c.tagline: Medieval walls cradling the Adriatic's most dramatic bay.

taxi.color: No uniform color (mixed private fleets); look for "TX" on the plate
taxi.fareNote: Meters run about €0.60-1/km, rising toward €1.30/km on the coast in summer; a fixed price agreed upfront is common and often better value in high season.

emergency.note: General EU-style number 112 also reaches emergency services; fire brigade is 123.

hood_desc: The medieval walled core of Kotor, packed with stone squares, cafes, and cruise-ship day-trippers; ideal for first-timers who want everything walkable and car-free, though it gets loud and crowded in peak season.
A long seafront promenade of former sea-captains' mansions just north of the walls, with parking and quieter nights; suits travelers wanting easy walking access to Old Town without the crowds.
A tiny, car-free Baroque village further into the bay near the Our Lady of the Rocks islet; best for a slow one- or two-night romantic stopover rather than a full-trip base.
An elegant, little-visited waterfront village about 4.5km from Kotor lined with grand 18th-century villas turned boutique hotels; suits travelers with a car seeking quiet upscale seclusion.
A narrow fishing hamlet directly across the bay from the Old Town with some of the best photo views of the walls and mountains; good for those prioritizing scenery over nightlife.

water.note: Generally safe and drunk by locals daily, though it can turn cloudy and undrinkable briefly after heavy winter storms.

transit.pay: Local Blue Line buses are pay-as-you-board in cash (small euro coins or notes); intercity coach tickets are bought at the station kiosk or from the driver. The Kamenari–Lepetane car/passenger ferry across the bay is paid in cash at the tollbooth on boarding (pedestrians ride free).
transit.hours: Local buses run roughly 6am-9pm with no night service; intercity coaches operate through early evening. The bay ferry runs around the clock at 10-15 minute intervals.
transit.note: Kotor's Old Town is entirely pedestrian, so most visitors walk everywhere and only use buses, the ferry, or taxis for trips along the bay or to nearby towns.

train: No rail line serves Kotor; nearest stations are in Podgorica or Bar on the Bar–Belgrade railway, reached by road transfer
bus: Intercity coaches to Podgorica, Budva, Herceg Novi, Nikšić, Dubrovnik, Belgrade, Sarajevo
ferry: Kamenari–Lepetane car/passenger ferry across the Bay of Kotor

transit.m: Local town bus via nearby Tivat center (infrequent, ~30-40 min incl. walk/transfer)

tip.r: A modest 5-10% for good restaurant service is appreciated; rounding up for taxis and cafes is common but not expected.

landmarks: Kotor Cathedral (St. Tryphon's Cathedral)
A Romanesque Catholic cathedral consecrated in 1166 and rebuilt with twin bell towers after the 1667 earthquake, holding a gilded silver altar screen and a reliquary chapel of Kotor's patron saint.
Kotor City Walls and St. John's Fortress
Four and a half kilometres of Venetian-era fortifications zigzagging 1,350 steps up the cliff behind the old town to a ruined fortress, with the bay spread out below at the top.
Church of St. Luke

A small Romanesque-Byzantine church from 1195 that served Catholic and Orthodox congregations simultaneously for centuries, its floor still paved with the gravestones of the medieval families who built it.
Square of the Arms (Trg od Oružja)
Kotor's main square, named for the Venetian armoury that once stood here, framed by the clock tower, the old rector's palace and the pillar of shame where wrongdoers were publicly displayed.
Sea Gate (Vrata od Mora)
The old town's principal entrance, cut through the walls in 1555 under Venetian rule, carrying a Venetian lion, a socialist-era relief and Tito's proclamation of Kotor's 1944 liberation.
Maritime Museum of Montenegro

A three-storey baroque palace housing ship models, navigational instruments, weapons and portraits documenting the Bay of Kotor's centuries as one of the Adriatic's most powerful seafaring communities.
Napoleon's Theatre
The first theatre in the Balkans, opened in 1810 during French rule in a converted palace on the main square, now part of the Hotel Cattaro with the original auditorium preserved.
Cats Museum of Kotor
A small museum of postcards, prints and posters devoted to the stray cats that have become the town's mascot, with proceeds funding the sterilisation and care of Kotor's street cats.
Church of St. Nicholas
A Serbian Orthodox church completed in 1909 in neo-Byzantine style, its dark interior lined with a tall gilded iconostasis and silver icons, one of the newest buildings inside the medieval walls.
Our Lady of the Rocks
A man-made islet off Perast, built up over centuries by sailors dropping stones after each safe voyage, crowned by a blue-domed church whose walls carry 68 baroque paintings by Tripo Kokolja.

dom.op: Železnički prevoz Crne Gore (ŽPCG) - nearest stations Bar and Sutomore

train.note: No railway reaches the Bay of Kotor - the line from Belgrade ends at Bar, and Sutomore is the closest station to the bay, roughly 40-60 km away over the coast road. From Bar, ZPCG trains run inland to Podgorica in about an hour and on through the mountains to Bijelo Polje and Belgrade, with the overnight Belgrade service the main international link. Most rail travellers arrive at Bar off that train and finish the journey to Kotor by bus in around 1.5-2 hours. Tickets are bought at station counters; the domestic fares are very cheap.

bus.note: Kotor's bus station (Autobuska stanica) is a five-minute walk south of the old town by the Gurdic gate. Regional buses leave for Budva every 30 minutes for about EUR 2.50 and for Podgorica hourly at around EUR 7.50, while international coaches serve Dubrovnik (roughly 2.5-3 hours, several a day), Mostar, Sarajevo, Split, Belgrade and Skopje. Buy at the station counter or online through BusTicket4.me (https://www.busticket4.me/); expect a small station fee and about EUR 1 per item of hold luggage. The Croatian border at Debeli Brijeg is a Schengen entry point and coach queues there can be long in July and August.

intl.to: Kamenari-Lepetane (Montenegro) - car ferry across the Verige narrows, about 25 km west of Kotor by road, ~10 min, runs 24 hours
intl.op: Kamenari-Lepetane ferry — pay at the ramp

intl.to: Perast, Our Lady of the Rocks & Herceg Novi (Montenegro) - taxi boats and seasonal excursion boats from the Kotor waterfront
intl.op: local boat operators — tickets at the quay

ferry.note: There are no scheduled ferries to Kotor itself; the town is a cruise port, with ships berthing right beside the medieval walls, and small taxi boats work the bay in summer. The genuinely useful crossing is the Kamenari-Lepetane car ferry over the mouth of the inner bay, which takes about ten minutes, runs around the clock without booking and saves roughly half an hour driving between Herceg Novi and Tivat or Budva. International sailings use Bar rather than Kotor - Adria Ferries has operated a seasonal Ancona-Bar service in some recent years, but it has not been on sale every season, so check before planning around it. Vehicle space on any Adriatic crossing needs booking well ahead in high summer.
